Quote: Twistkill, 2007-09-05T22:47:08Z
Part of the reason for extreme heat is because of all the smog covering up the atmosphere and created the greenhouse effect.
While there are areas where the current temperature increase (about 0.7 C) makes a difference (South Africa, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, the edges of Andean and Alpine glaciers), the Sacramento River valley has been plain old hot for centuries. Now, in a city, the excess heat generated by power consumption comes into play, but not so much in a small town.
However, with a recent near-doubling of population in the valley, power consumption has increased dramatically. Air conditioners use a massive amount of energy, and Carnot's theorem implies that they always will. "Solutions" might include better insulation-aerogel seems promising, but it's not manufactured in large quantities yet, and solar panels, which can't power a house, but can offset some of the energy consumption.
The word "solution" is in quotation marks because it's not a true solution-it's not more energy, it's a way to use what's available.
#362790 17 2007-09-06T23:13:28Z scythe33
Quote: 321southpaw, September 06, 2007 09:19 pm

I read something in the back of The Sun magazine yesterday in the Sunbeams section (and I'm also paraphrasing):

Solar power will never be considered by power companies because nobody owns the sun.


You're aware that The Sun is a tabloid, right?
Anyway, solar power can't be considered by power companies, because with a 20% efficient (and that's considered good) solar panel, it would take approximately 100 square miles of solar panels to power a small town. Now, there's plenty of room in America to get far, far more than we need, but definitely not in densely populated areas like the New York-Philadelphia region or the Sacramento river valley. Solar panels can be considered a supplement to the power of a single-family home, but unless massive efficiency gains are realized (not so much in the panels as in the home appliances the panels run), solar panels on the roof can't power a house alone.
So they're a supplement. And no, it's not run by a power company, because it is free and requires very little maintenance. However, solar panels *are* available for purchase to the general public.
Using a generous limit from Wikipedia, let's say we obtain 40 W/m. If your house is 100 feet by 100 feet, that translates to 30mx30m, or 900 m. Our total electric wattage produced is therefore 36kW for eight hours a day (again, a generous number), so 288 kWh/day.
Now, an average home consumes somewhere around 4MJ/m-day (actually, it's somewhat higher in the US. Energy consumption in Sweden, however, averages less than half this number), or 1.11kWh/m-day, so our 900 square meter house consumes about 1000 kWh/day (isn't that a convenient number). Even in Sweden, the average consumption per day is around 400 kWh/day for a house of this size, and that assumes it's one story. (More importantly, in Sweden, the sunlight is at a very indirect angle meaning that even less energy is available to the unfortunate homeowner, not to mention the 4 hour days in the winter).
In short, no, you can't power a house like that, unless we, say, outdo Sweden. Hey, it's just Sweden, right? We can do better than that.

#17258 1 2007-09-18T04:20:09Z scythe33
This is that huge essay I was working on a few nights ago, fully revised (sorta), and ready to turn in (actually, after the teacher evaluates it, we make a few minor changes)
Read, enjoy, and please, any suggestions for improvement are greatly appreciated!

On May 12, 1998, massive riots sparked by shootings at a student demonstration overtook the Indonesian capital city of Jakarta on the island of Java, and became a pogrom directed at people of Chinese descent. Much speculation exists about the causes of the riots, and whether the Indonesian army and government supported the riots-what is known is that during the riots, much of Jakarta descended into anarchy. Massive gangs began roaming the city, breaking, entering, and looting buildings, mainly those owned by or occupied by people of Chinese descent, often referred to as the ethnic Chinese, who were targeted because many are well-off, which is resented by the Indonesian ethnic majority, a situation similar to pre-World War II Germany. Many ethnic Chinese were killed, and a substantial number of Chinese women and girls were violently raped. After the riots, independent investigations repeatedly indicated that sections of the Indonesian military were actively involved in planning and executing the riots. This was denied by the Indonesian army; however, evidence indicates that the military was indeed involved in the riots.
The riots were carried out in protest against the government of President Suharto of Indonesia. Suharto was responsible for the pseudo-fascist New Order in Indonesia which was responsible for numerous human-rights violations. Suharto also presided over high unemployment and inflation, food shortages, and rampant corruption in the government. The riots were part of the Indonesian Revolution of 1998, in which Suharto was removed from office, and ended with the installation of President Habibe, a little-known man with so many academic qualifications that BBC News remarked that he has a fetish for academic titles. At the time he took power, BBC compared him to Napoleon, Francisco Franco, and Haile Selassie, but his rule, while corrupt, was not as draconian as that of the aforementioned leaders. In this sense, the riots may be considered a success in that they finally deposed a corrupt official; however, the death toll and massive injustices incurred implies that the ends most certainly did not justify the means.
Minor rioting had been a problem in Jakarta in 1997 and early 1998. Indeed, in early 1998, fear was common among ethnic Chinese in Jakarta that a repeat of the ethnic violence that claimed thousands of lives in the 1960s was immanent. Animosity toward ethnic Chinese was caused by the view that they are more loyal to China than they are to Indonesia; these views were reinforced by Chinas policy until the late 1980s of awarding citizenship to ethnic Chinese born in Indonesia and other areas of Southeast Asia. The most prominent evidence that the preceding minor riots had a racial element was some shopkeepers practice of putting up signs on the store window reading Belonging to an Indonesian. Most such shops were left untouched by rioters.
In the month before the riots, there were dozens of student protests and demonstrations against the corrupt regime of then-Indonesian President Suharto occurring throughout Indonesia. Since the late 1980s, pressure had been building on Suharto, who had ruled Indonesia since 1966, to resign. Supporters cited reports of corruption. His re-appointment in March of 1998 strengthened these views. The final spark occurred during a student demonstration at Triskati University in Jakarta when police opened fire on student demonstrators. Rioting broke out and spread like an oil spill; by May 13th, almost all of Jakarta had descended into anarchy.
Although the riots were carried out in protest of the government, racial tension and military intervention quickly turned the riots against the ethnic Chinese (descendants of Chinese immigrants to Indonesia), similar to Kristallnacht in Germanyshops owned by ethnic Chinese had their windows smashed in and were looted, homes of ethnic Chinese were raided, and many ethnic Chinese were killed. One major divergence from the similarity to Kristallnacht were the mass rapes-many of which were not reported until several years after the riots, and which the government refused to acknowledge had occurred. One anecdote later made public told of how rioters gathered around an apartment building which housed many Chinese, entered, and raped at least 50 of the occupants.
The non-human causes of the Jakarta riots included food shortages, unemployment, and human rights violations. According to BBC News, Indonesia before 1998 was ...a society which never shows its feelings and it did so with a vengeance, in what was literally an orgy of violence. The riots were reportedly sparked during a student protest at Triskati University in Jakarta when Indonesian military officers opened fire. Though the government has not acknowledged it, it is possible that the shooting was intended to start a riot; the Volunteer Team for Humanity notes that much of the destruction was carried out in a similar, almost carefully planned matter, and asks how can coincidence explain the similarity of the weird fact pattern, that the destroy/burning action invitor-leader didnt take a part in the plunder act. Even in many cases, the invitor-leader immediately left the mass who start to move themselves to destroy and plunder. (sic). This implies that a smaller, more informed group of people were actively influencing the riots, and causing them to occur in the manner that they did; rampant corruption in the military is a very likely cause.
One of the most notable causes-alternatively, one of the most obvious-of the poor economic situation in Indonesia was the 1997 East Asian financial crisis. Beginning with the collapse of the Thai baht in July 1997, many East Asian countries, including Thailand, South Korea, and Indonesia entered a severe economic depression that lasted over a year, and spread to other countries in Asia, including Russia, as well as to Latin America. As a result of the crisis, the currency of many Southeast Asian countries fell, and the rapid development prior to the crisis stalled. The crisis drove already severe unemployment higher, and fueled rising discontent in Indonesia.
The 1997 East Asian financial crisis was similar to a 19th-century era bank run; investors quickly attempted to remove their money from what they suddenly saw as an unstable East Asian market. These feelings of instability may have been compounded by the 1997 British surrender of Hong Kong to China, since the fate of that powerful economy was as of yet unknown. This insecurity, plus the recent raise in US interest rates following the end of the economic recession of the early 1990s, began to draw investors away from East Asian markets. This came to a climax in Thailand in 1997, when the Thai baht was attacked by speculators and soon collapsed. A domino effect extended to the rest of the East Asian market, including Malaysia and Indonesia.
While the principal causes were economic woes, discontent with the Suharto regime had been festering since the 1960s; however, with the collapse of the Soviet Union, Western powers were no longer afraid of Indonesia becoming a communist state and therefore did not worry as much about angering the Indonesian government. Since the West no longer looked favorably on Suhartos culling of his opponents, many of Indonesias youth grew more vocal about their dissatisfaction with the Suharto regime. Discontent with Suharto became especially prevalent following the 1997 East Asian financial crisis. Historically, many Indonesians had tolerated the Suharto regime, despite corruption and human-rights abuses, because Suhartos regime had brought prosperity to many Indonesians and good economic development to the country as a whole. However, when this prosperity was shattered in the financial crisis, Suhartos public support quickly declined. This was boosted when Suharto was reappointed again in March 1998, and protests spread against the Suharto regime, eventually leading up to the fateful Triskati protest.
So what made the riots spread so quickly? One theory is that Major-General Prabowo Subianto, Suhartos son-in-law, ordered his troops to encourage the riots, which he could then blame on General Wiranto, the Indonesian Chief of Staff. An official investigation into the riots indicated that the Indonesian army had attempted something akin to a coup detat-whether it was for or against the Suharto regime was not revealed, and possibly not understood. In any case, most of the people of Jakarta had been severely discontent for the past several months, and most were quick to take any action against anyone in the hope of changing something. At times, bystanders joined marching student demonstrators, and the demonstrations quickly disintegrated into mob action, with looting, burning, and attacks on innocent people. In one instance, a witness reported people being offered money to join in the riots-since money was scarce; many of those people had very little choice in the matter.
Some important evidence that the military was involved in planning and executing the riots was that the riots were carried out against ethnic Chinese. Presumably, a group of rioters dissatisfied with the government would attack government buildings, unless they were externally influenced otherwiseplus, someone influencing them to not attack government buildings and officials most likely has a stake in the security of the government. Indeed, in the beginning of the rioting, it was carried out almost exclusively against military and police cars and offices. For example, rioters attacked a car dealership displaying Bimantara sedans, which (Bimantara) was partially owned by Suhartos son-in-law. However, the ethnic Chinese were quickly made scapegoats of and the riots turned against them, partially because they, too, like Suhartos family, were well-off.
The police, intentionally or not, exacerbated the riots; in one instance, the police ...clubbed students and journalists as they fled the scene, clogging rush-hour traffic. Bystanders joined the student protesters who hurled rocks at the police. It is likely that high-ranking officials discontent with Suharto ordered this to instigate a mass riot, or even a revolt. Two main officials implicated for this are Major General Prabowo and Major General Sjafrie Samsuddin. Major-General Prabowo, in particular, is considered to have played a key role in causing the riots. One theory is that one of the two generals instigated the riots in an attempt to discredit the other; if this is true, it could well have been Samsuddin and Prabowo is innocent.
Despite powerful evidence for military involvement, it is known that the military was not responsible for all of the rioting; in one area of the city, rioting began when high school students, marching behind a banner reading Down With Suharto asked passers-by to join them-and abruptly, they deteriorated into a mob, throwing stones at anything breakable[8]. When police arrived on the scene, the area was littered with glass [8] and police fired shots into the air, causing the members of the mob to split up and flee into side streets. In other areas, police attempts to breakup rioting mobs were not as successful, and in at least one instance, students and bystanders threw rocks at riot police. In some documented cases, disgruntled riot police joined the rioters.
The government-led investigations into the riots as well as Indonesian statements about the riots in the first few days after the riots were patently false. Initially, Indonesian government officials repeatedly denied that any rapes occurred during the riots; according to the Human Rights Watch, On June 29th, armed forces commander General Wiranto gave a press conference and stated that the military had gone to twenty hospitals that had treated victims of the May riots. Of 630 victims, twelve had died, eighty-seven had been kept in for treatment, and the rest were able to go home, but there was not a single case of rape. However, on July 3, the Indonesian minister for womens affairs, Tutty Alawiyah, acknowledged that rapes had indeed taken place, contradicting earlier statements, and implying that the government almost certainly knew about the rapes before then, and definitely knew about the issue by June 29th. On July 7, a spokesman for the Indonesian National Commission on Human Rights stated that We can say without any doubt whatsoever that on those dates [May 13-15] mass rape of ethnic Chinese women occurred that was widespread, systematic, and sadistic. (Human Rights Watch).
Despite admission by several branches of government that rapes had occurred during the riots, the government continued to deny that any raping of ethnic Chinese women had occurred even through August 1998. The Human Rights Watch reports that By August 17, the national police commander, General Roesmanhadi, was threatening to prosecute the organizations that had been most vocal in publicizing the rape issue on charges of spreading false rumors. Government claims that there were no rapes were strengthened by revelations that some of the photographs of rape that were posted on the Internet had actually been copied photographs from earlier violence in East Timor-others had even been stolen from pornographic websites. It is possible that such photographs were fabricated by people who wished to conceal the rapes or hide them; nonetheless, the body of evidence that implies a campaign of mass rape is far larger than simply those photographs. However, it was later generally agreed that mass rape actually did occur.
After the riots, at first, many ethnic Chinese rape victims were reluctant to come forward, and one of the main places that many came forward was in churches. Many ethnic Chinese are Christian, and they overcame their shame at church. One young girl told of how a gang of rioters invaded the apartment building where she lived, which was populated with mostly ethnic Chinese. Despite trying to evade the rioters, and offering money for the rioters to leave her and her family alone, she, her sister, and her aunt were gang raped by the rioters; her sister and her uncle were stabbed to death. A hospital worker said that she knew of at least 400 cases of rape-indicating that far more ethnic Chinese were raped than those that came forward.
The government cover-up for the rapes is one of the single most powerful pieces of evidence of government and military involvement in the riots-after all, theres no reason to hide something that somebody else did. However, government officials repeatedly denied that any rapes had occurred until July 3, when the Indonesian government essentially did an about-face-the Indonesian minister for Womens Affairs acknowledged that rapes had taken place, and said that making the victims feel more secure was more important than raising evidence-which, despite being true, is still a weighted statement in that she tries to avoid making a case for an international investigation of the riots. Even after this, the government still tried to paint the picture that no rapes had occurred. On August 17, General Roesmanhadi, the Indonesian national police commander, threatened to prosecute the organizations which had been the most instrumental in publicizing the rape issue on charges of spreading false rumors. Other Indonesian government associations quickly followed suit, and before long the official government position was that no rapes occurred in the riots.
While many well-documented and supported cases indicate that police and military actions may have angered some of the rioters, and possibly did so intentionally, evidence that the government and military actively supported the riots is anecdotal at best, but reports are common enough that it is doubtful they are all false. One Tim Richardson reports that his fiances father was traveling in a small bus when traffic ground to a halt due to the outbreak of the riots. He and his fellow passengers decided to complete their trip on foot. An elderly man, he rested frequently during his two kilometres walk. In that time, he saw empty trucks travelling along the road, recruiting young men with the promise of 20,000 Rupiah to join the riots (the minimum monthly wage is about 150,000 Rupiah). While not confirmed, stories like this are not likely to be fabricated-after all, there is little gain for the storyteller by telling the story, and thus are good evidence that such events actually occurred. Plus, since most such retellings share similar elements, and generally agree with each other, it is likely that the events described happened-it is doubtful, for example, that several people will all fabricate what is essentially the same event.
Although the riots occurred nine years ago, most of the leaders and rioters are still unknown; the only accused riot leader was President Suhartos son-in-law, Major-General Prabowo Subianto. This strongly implies a planned riot; impromptu riot leaders would not have had loyal subsidiaries and would have been easily captured after the riots had ended. Also, it implies that the government, even that of President Habibe, was somewhat sympathetic to the rioters-a more focused investigation almost assuredly would have turned up more information than the Indonesian government released.
Investigation into the riots was mostly led by the newly-formed Indonesian National Human Rights Commission, though the Indonesian government has been slow to react to its findings. The NHRC operates more or less independently; despite having no true power, it exercises power in the form of press releases that may put pressure on the government to respond. When the NHRC investigated the May riots, the finding that many ethnic Chinese were raped and the calls for a national investigative commission were at first accepted by President Habibe, and in July, the government set up an investigative commission, presumably a nod to the NHRC. However, in August, many public officials had begun questioning whether any rapes actually occurred, in blind ignorance of the NHRCs findings. The NHRC was the only organization permitted to investigate the Jakarta riots; according to the US Department of State, The [Indonesian] Government generally considers outside investigations or foreign-based criticism of alleged human rights violations to be interference in its internal affairs. It emphasizes its belief that the linkage of foreign assistance, or other sanctions, to its human rights observance constitutes interference in its internal affairs and is therefore unacceptable.
All investigations, news reports, and anecdotes considered, the evidence strongly points to a riot made possible by a severe economic downturn, aided and abetted by the military of Indonesia. The riots, sparked by the shooting of student protesters at Triskati University in Jakarta, quickly consumed much of the unfortunate city, and became an outlet for pent-up resentment towards the Indonesian government and ethnic Chinese living in Jakarta. The riots, while planned by the military, were soon out of the militarys control, and mobs of angry rioters began roaming the streets, breaking into shops, looting things which they did not need, and breaking and entering the homes of ethnic Chinese, destroying much of what was in the homes, and raping the female occupants. Ethnic Chinese were a target for the riots because similar to the Jews in Weimar Germany, they were a prosperous minority in an economic depression. They lived generally together, and were seen as being more loyal to their native China than to Indonesia.
The rioters rioted because their lives at the time were miserable. A severe economic recession and the recent reappointment of who was essentially a dictator, then-President Suharto, had filled the Jakartan barrel with plenty of gunpowder. They rioted when they did and where they did because of the men holding the strings, the men with the guns. Disagreements in the Indonesian military had made it desirable for any one of the high ranking generals to try and oust the others, so as to get more of their allies in the military into high-ranking positions. In the end, the riots succeeded in doing what both the rioters, and the puppet-masters, had intended: disposal of the aging dictator Suharto, but at a cost far higher than anyone had imagined.

Well, first it was any number of things. When I was young, I gave myself the moniker "yoop". I don't know where that came from. Eventually I saw "blade" used as a name, so for myself, I stuck "scythe" onto it, making "scytheblade". When I first discovered razoric.com (which is now either defunct or very changed from what it was originally), the character |DG|H4x0r on the mario/resident evil video gave me the idea of adding _hax onto the end. It became scytheblade_hax. I still use the _hax ending for character names in games like Diablo, where you can have more than one character per account.
When I took up Diablo, scytheblade_hax wouldn't fit in the account name selection. I dropped it to scythe, which was taken, so I added 33, trying to keep my username under eight characters for some reason I no longer remember-otherwise it would have been 333. This was all well and good-I named my first character scytheblade_hax, and kept using it. When I came to the battle.net forums in late 2003, the name attached to me was now "Scythe33". I played around with the capitalization, variously "Scythe33", "ScYtHe33", and "scythe33". It wasn't until a few years later that I finally decided it looked more "stylish" with a lowercase s. #371551 36 2007-10-12T21:29:21Z scythe33
Does my attempt to defy any pattern create a pattern in itself? It certainly would seem so, yet such an attempt itself can lead to essentially all possible responses. However, these do not have equal probabilities; it may be said that my attempts not to conform to a pattern of posting lead to a probability distribution over the space of possible posts. However, this is not a pattern; a pattern usually gives a single expected post, and most patterns change with time. This distribution is generally independent of my previous post, or at least the correlation with it is quite small. In this sense, my posting may be considered a sort of Markov chain that attempts to approximate the truly unpredictable [1/n 1/n 1/n ... 1/n] distribution with n elements as my post count increases. Therefore, to minimize predictability, I should post as often as possible for as long as possible. But is this itself predictable, can the lack of a post be considered a possibility in the set of posts? I don't know. I'm going to make the assumption, though, that nobody predicted this.

At speeds above 60 miles per hour, the energy requirement goes up roughly as the square of the speed, because drag becomes more significant than other forms of resistance. Specifically, if you get 42 mpg at 60 mph (Volkswagen Jetta TDI), you'll get about 34 mpg at 70 mph, and 28 mpg at 80 mph-both of which are lower than the TDI's city mileage of 35 mpg (though that assumes 45 mph travel).
However, it's generally a good idea not to let driving bore you. If you're interested in what you're doing, you'll do it better several nines of the time. I drive fast. But you probably already knew that, didn't you?

Addicts are some of the most victimized people in soceity; we look at them unfailingly as people who have lost something. And without drifting too far into Brave New World, it's ironic that most people would be unsatisfied with eternal happiness. There is no key to happiness that can be given without changing something about yourself-often, giving up a part of who you are. I might well just be blathering here. There are two commonly portrayed types of happy people-the idea of "life in the fast lane", where life has so many changes you can't help but forget about things that are behind you, and the idea emphasized by such groups as patagonia, which is just the opposite of that-yet, many outside observers looks on either version as if that type of person is missing out on something essential to life. We drive ourselves away from these lifestyles, not towards them, and that's not easy to reconcile. Yet we do tend more towards the former near college years, and the latter as we age-and a common symptom of aging is wishing to recover that which we left behind, the midlife crisis. If I were Plato, I'd have to give up here. But I'm an idiot, so I can keep typing and hope I get somewhere even though I won't. And damned if I'm the first to say it, but we have at least in the past admired tragedy. Learn to look at the pitfalls in your life and take them as a reminder that you're still alive. #382476 2 2007-11-24T02:18:26Z scythe33
Quote: aries_griff, 2005-12-25T05:22:09Z
Ok, the first part (the top) is pretty simple, just don't get killed on the mines. I recommend getting the switch, but it's not actually necessary; you can run through that top part(just hold right all the way and you'll get it) and bounce off the ledge(right by where the platform would appear) and if you have your momentum going, you'll bounce right over the mines. Oh, and watch out for the drone. Easy enough, I shouldn't have to explain anything about it if you've made it this far in the game.

I'll do the rest of this thwump by thwump, or corridor by corridor(where a corridor is like one straight section that ends when the level turns)

The very first thwump is easy. Just jump straight at it, and it will go down, and you will go over. I try to aim to land on the small flat ledge a little to the right of the first thwump.

Standing on that ledge triggers a thwump to come upwards towards you. Don't worry about it, there's enough room on the left side for you to fall safely while it's coming at you. So go ahead and tiptoe off the right side of the ledge and fall straight down. If you fall straight off the ledge and don't move either direction, the thwump will pass you, and you will land on a slanted ledge which will send you to the right side of the corridor onto another slanted ledge that will send you right on top of another thwump(it faces left). So for that falling part, just fall straight off that little ledge(you may have to realign yourself by tapping left once or twice) and don't press anything til you hit that slant that's about 45 degrees in the lower right corner that shoots you on top of the thwump(if all went right). At that point(and maybe a little before you hit the ledge), start moving left. *Alternatively*, if you're not planning to run on top of the thwump in the bottom left, you can take this part a little slower, dropping from ledge to ledge and land in the bottom right where it's safe, so you can get ready for your slow trek across the bottom(I don't like that way).

Start moving left because I found the easiest way to do this part is to just keep running on top of the thwump(really not that hard after the first or second try and it flows really well). Then jump before the thwump coming at you kills you (you should be jumping right after the first of two arches of gold). There should be a raised part in the ceiling right there for you to clear the oncoming thwump, and a flat, raised ledge(with no mines on it) for you to land on. From that ledge, you have to either teeter over the edge(so the ninja isn't standing straight up) or actually be on the slant to jump safely, because there's an overhanging slanted ceiling to block your jump(and send you into the mines) if you jump too high. You should land on a slant that faces towards you, so jump once you land on it or run left off of it, or you'll slide into a mine. So land on that flat part, or the slant next to the mine(you may have landed on them anyways if you jumped far enough), which are right next to the slight slant that faces right, which is where you landed, and jump left. I like to land on the right side of the piece of the floor that kinda looks like a ^ sign and jump into the little crevice above that big vertical piece of wall. You can chill there or wallslide/jump/wallslide that wall below it for a bit if you need to catch your breath, just don't get squashed by a thwump coming back. *ALTERNATIVELY*, if you're shy about riding thwumps, the bottom part is doable just jumping through, it's just tricky. But if you're not riding on top of the thwumps, I would recommend riding on the side of the thwump that comes at you. You can do this by letting it come at you while you chill in the mine-less bottom right corner. Once it hits the wall, jump and wallslide its left side, and keep jumping and holding right, and you should be able to ride the sucker all the way to the little crevice. It takes awhile, but you should have plenty of time.

The decision is how to do this next part. Some people will jump off, land on the slant facing the wall on the ^ shaped part, jump to the wall, wall jump up, then wall jump the teeny vertical ledges. Personally, I always thought that was hard. So I like to chill in the little crevice, then hop up onto that baby corner right above it(yes, it's right next to the mines, so watch out). You don't need to stand on the ledge, you can just land the corner and jump immediately before you fall off. When you jump to the right off that corner, a lot of the time you'll have to walljump off that tiny vertical ledge that's there top hop of to the flat ledge, where you can chill. Jump to the next ledge up, and don't worry about the switch(it's useless IMHO). Then jump up to the slanted part right above that ledge and chill.

This next part has a lot of variation, but I'll tell you what I find easiest. Highscorers jump further right and let the thwump go over them while they cut it close on a slant next to a mine, which is very hard, so I don't recommend. I recommend chilling on that slant you are on, above the ledges and hopping and holding right, so the thwump triggers and goes right over your head(with a significant amount of room). Then jump on the right side of the thwump(it's back) and wallslide/jump/wallslide by jumping and holding left the entire time. You can hold on as long as you want, and depending on where you get off the thwump, your strategy changes a little. I like getting off of the thwump somewhere around the terminal switch, and I usually do it by jumping high on one of my wall slide jumps, landing on top of the thwump and jumping so it goes under me(or just clearing it with the first jump). You can do this pretty safely right before or right after the terminal switch(I prefer before, because you have more landing room). Then I wait in that flat area to the right of the terminal(you can wait on any surface you like, just don't get killed, and make sure theres a high ceiling) and when the thwump come back at me, I jump over it, let it go under(I usually land on the 45 degree right facing slant to the right of the terminal) , then make the rest of my jumps. I jump from that 45 degree slant to the next small gap in the mines, a smaller slant that faces left, and then I hop (I think it's safer than a full jump) to the small flat gap between mines. Then I hop over to the slanted corner and wait(hop and wait, so I don't fall immediately).

This next part(next 2 corridors) is extremely difficult, and there's no way around it that I found. My favorite way to do it is very hard, but so is every other way. You have to trigger that thwump facing upwards by leaning over the edge or hopping. Then when it hits the top, fall off the ledge under it. There are three slants you can land on, and each has a way to survive.

This is where it gets extremely difficult. You can pick which ledge to land on, I'll explain each, and I'll put a number for each so you can know when I talk about each. I like to land on the ledge on the left (the steepest one), so I'll start by explaining that.
(*1*) When you fall, land directly on the ledge, which will require a little steering, because if you fall straight down, you won't be far enough left to hit it. With the momentum of your fall, jump as soon as you hit the ledge, which is very hard, and then land in the small gap between mines (there's a flat part and a slanted part, but it's tough to land in that area because of the speed). Depending on how fast you were going and where you jump from, you will 9 times out of ten need to hold right to slow down your jump so you don't overshoot that small gap. Then jump immediately when you land to avoid the thwump coming from the left straight at you. You can jump straight up and come back down or you can jump up and left to the next piece of floor clear of mines, which is three mines away from where you landed. From there, just keep jumping from one small clearing to another til you are on that ledge at the end of the corridor(the jumps are hard, I know, but there's nothing I can do to help you with that). *Alternatively*, once you jump over the thwump that comes from the left side towards you, you can wait til it comes back and ride the left side of it to the ledge like I have previously described.
(*2*) Landing on the slant on the far right instead of the slant I talked about earlier is much the same. I don't like it because you have to watch out for the mines to even get to the slant to land on it, and once you land on it, the jump is harder. Anyways, once you land on the small slant on the right, do the exact jump as I described earlier, to the gap between a set of 3 mines and a set of 4 mines. Only now, the jump is farther. I have done this, so I know it is possible, but I think it's harder (personal opinion).
(*3*) The middle ledge. You might think it's easier, because you don't have to jump right when you land on it, and for some it will be. Since you can't jump left with enough speed to beat the thwump coming towards you when you land in the middle, your only choice is to wait for the thwumps to come to you. On the other ledges, you didn't have to worry about when the timing with vertical thwump coming back down, but for this one it may make a big difference. The idea for this ledge is to wait for the vertical thwump to come back down, and jump up and left off your ledge into that little gap between the mine and the vertical thwump before it traps you. If you wait for the vertical thwump at the top of the descent, so that when you fall to this middle ledge, you barely beat the thwump coming back down(so you are pretty close to getting smashed between the corner you fall from and the thwump coming back down), if you do that, what happens is that the vertical thwump is closer to resetting when the thwump coming from the left triggers. This allows you enough time to trigger the vertical thwump again by jumping up and left(you may like to jump to the left-facing 45 degree slant to left of the middle slant to prevent being trapped) and so when that vertical thwump triggers for the second time, the left-right thwump goes underneath you. Then you can either ride that thwump over to the ledge on the left side of the corner, or wait in one of the safe parts and let it go under you, or you can go faster through this horizontal corridor than the thwump does coming back. The point is, if you can delay the thwump coming from the left triggering, it makes this easier, and the basic idea is get the vertical thwump out of the corner and make it so you don't have to deal with that thwump coming fast at you from the left. It's a tricky jump triggering the vertical thwump from that lower right corner so that the left-right thwump doesn't kill you, but you may find it easier than executing the jumps from the other ledges.

Any way you do that last part, it's probably going to be very hard, and you end up on the small ledge on the left part of the corridor. This vertical corridor is small and nothing happens in it, so I recommend gathering your thoughts and focusing for the last part, which is hard. Just jump your way to that top small slant that faces right, and get ready.

The last part is the most intense. You start from that little slant at the start of the corridor(the thwump won't trigger yet, so don't worry). The next jumps are precision jumps that require skill and speed. From that slant, jump to the SECOND gap in the mines (theres a piece of gold over each gap). The second one is MUCH easier to hit for me, and it makes clearing the thwump easy. The thwump triggers as you land, so from that second gap, jump high and to the right a little, and follow the ceiling to land in the last gap in the mines. Then jump high and to the right again, and follow the ceiling again right to the door. Congrats, you made it!

[/easy way]
That's Aries' 2000+ word essay on how to beat MTI. I don't think it'd be possible to do more than that.

Let's play hypotheticals. Let's assume that it really works. The life of all humans has just been extended by 40 years.
What happens next?
I thought it was an interesting question. If we look at some math:
Traditionally, aging starts around 35 (though the body is by no means exhausted at this point, and indeed it's well before halfway through the human lifespan). If the 50% claim holds for that marker, it moves up to 53. Of course, school still ends, for all intents and purposes, by 25 or so. That increases the gap between out-of-college and the end of athletic viability in most sports from 10 years to 28. Certainly, that'll be noticeable.

But how would we even distribute the stuff? Current supplements are known not to be sufficient-25 mg supplements don't raise the plasma level to what was effective in mice. Will this cause something akin to Dune, where everyone is effectively hooked on melange? Would-gasp-some people try to keep it for themselves (even though it literally grows on trees), as has happened with everything else in history, period?
Oh, and what would we do about all that?

#400975 17 2008-01-15T02:06:45Z scythe33
Quote: The_apprentice, January 13, 2008 10:52 pm
measuring significantly alters the result.
Quote: Wikipedia
In 1935, Einstein, Podolski and Rosen published an analysis of widely separated entangled particles. Measuring one particle, Einstein realized, would alter the probability distribution of the other, yet here the other particle could not possibly be disturbed. This example led Bohr to revise his understanding of the principle, concluding that the uncertainty was not the caused by a direct interaction
Not quite.
Let's say we have a camera with one piece of film on it. This is a magic camera; it takes a picture of the entire Universe at once. Now, there's one thing about the camera's measurement we can vary: the shutter duration. If the shutter is open for a short time, we know a lot about where the objects in our picture are. If it's open for more time, we know where they're going-they've formed streaks in the direction of their motion. But we can't measure both.
Now, that's not a perfect explanation, but it's a conception of the idea of uncertainty.

Quote: Skillz J. Majik Trim, January 18, 2008 07:39 pm
Actually, I wouldn't have gotten cancer no matter what I paid.

Oh, really now?
Let's have a look:


Now, the second graph is there for the amount of ozone at various altitudes. About 65% is above 20 km, no?
Let's play the hypothetical situation where we lose that 40% comfort zone. Now, we're looking at the DNA Action Spectra plus the amount of radiation-both are logarithmic. To simplify things, let's just use the wavelength at which DNA Action spectra intersects the intensity (very rough approximation of the total effect on DNA of the UV). At current levels, we're on the line marked "surface", which ranks about a 2 on the "DNA Action Spectra" and 10^-8 on the intensity, so we have a flux of 2*10^-8. If we lose that 35%, we're on the line marked 20 km. The maximum there ranks about a 4 in DNA action and about 10^-7 in intensity, so we have a flux of 4*10^-7, which is a twentyfold increase in radiation.

Now, melanoma cases occur in the US at a rate of about 60,000 cases a year. If all photons are equal, the rate should also increase twentyfold, to about 1.2 million a year. In seventy years-about a lifetime-that's about 84 million, which means that one in four Americans will get melanoma in their lifetimes.

So let's see when we'd hit that level.

The Protocol called for the phase-out of CFC's by 1996, so we'll look at the trends up until then. The average of the readings around 1980 was around 300 DU, and the average around 1996 was around 280 DU. A 35% decrease from 280 is 180, so at 10 per 8 years, we'd hit it in 80 years. Of course, that's not the way ozone depletion works; it's catalyzed by CFC's, so the rate of depletion would constantly increase as we used more and more of them. Plus, thanks to CFC's high global warming potential, the stratosphere would be cooled (a surprising effect of global warming), allowing for more holes to develop over more areas.
So what do we say to those people that get a hole?

Last but not least, CFC's, as I recall, aren't even that profitable. Other refrigerants like cyclopropane are cheaper to make, but flammable, so the government actually phased them out. I can't guarantee it, though.

Now, the formation of the short-lived but huge Mongol Empire is central here. From 900-1300, the Middle East was superior to the Europeans. The Islamic Golden Age ended right after the Mongol Invasion with the formation of the Ottoman Empire, which united the whole Middle East-but soon became tyrannical. France, Britain, and Spain were untouched by the Mongol invasion-but the black plague had started in Hungary. The Hundred Years War ended-and so for the next two hundred years, the Western Europeans continued in relative peace where the Arabs left off (China was still embroiled in wars). This leads up to Europe's discovery of the Carribean Islands. Now, the islanders were relatively primitive, having been isolated from the rest of the world-the motif here is that communication is power. So, the Europeans were able to quickly conquer areas of the Carribean, and they got rich. This led to plenty of advancement-mostly, the Europeans perfected sea travel. Also, Europe could grow food on the Carribean islands, which meant that food became available for more people-mostly in England and Spain. Plus, there's plenty of gold and silver, and the Americas are great for cotton. Now, slavery has occurred forever. Even as late as the 1700s, even white people could be enslaved in some areas of Europe. African empires wanted European goods-in trade, they offered the Europeans slaves. However, Europe still hasn't become a juggernaut.
All that allows Britain and France to take the plague, which has finally arrived, without the loss of life Hungary experienced (not that it was easy for Britain). Russia, too, has become powerful, but it's focus is the east. Then, the Enlightenment. Probably the only time Europe really pulled itself up by the bootstraps.

These claims that rap isn't musical are ridiculous. Of course it's musical, it just expands the boundary of what can be musical (think musique concrte.) The entire genesis of rap was founded on the fact that it wanted to be anti-commodity, anti-commercial music, a very post-modern concept. It proposed to use found sounds (often samples), over a repetitive musical minimalism (looping) while not singing, but rather, talking over the sounds, to create a new synthesis. This was a breakthrough as it conceptualized the idea of eternal songwritingthe fact that using music history one can produce even more music and re-contextualize it for an artist's own expression.

It is heavily ironic that rap went from anti-commodification to the number one product of modern mainstream music, but hey, I guess people don't mind the abstract as much as they protest against it.
That's not new. In fact, that's similar to the way Homer probably first recounted the Odyssey and the Iliad-very simple background and lyrical speech. Of course, the instruments used are more complicated, but the Simpsons still did it. Heck, so did the Irish bards of the 1500's.

Not that it's necessarily bad-it's just not new.

I support lowering it farther. That's partially because of where I live. Where I live, anybody can take a boat 50 miles offshore, and there it's legal over 18. I find it silly that something that's legal just 50 miles away is illegal here, ostensibly wrong de novo. In the end, who are we to tell people whether or not they can eat something? We can (and should) advise against it, but it comes down to a product that human beings have been able to make since prehistory. It's not some industrially synthesized, complex, artificial compound; it's a bunch of grape juice left to ferment.
It might very well be dumb, but you can't legislate intelligence. Hell, do you think there would be all the hoopla surrounding alcohol if we treated it like caffeine? Nobody, and I mean freaking nobody goes to a bar and drinks twelve Coca-Colas. Nobody even gets to five Cokes. Yet we have people who go to bars nightly to drink nearly twenty bottles of beer. It's the culture that surrounds it; the fact that the government surrounds alcohol with a bureaucracy, makes it an activity, because you have to jump through hoops to get it.
And yes, alcohol is addictive. Caffeine is also addictive, in larger amounts. You can't get addicted to caffeine drinking one or two Cokes a day. You can, however, get addicted to caffeine if you drink three or four espressos in a day. The same (mostly) goes for alcohol. I know few people who drink a beer a day and can't stop themselves. I know too many that drink twelve.

Quote: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_communication_theorem
Theorem. In a Bell test, the statistics of Bob's measurements are unaffected by anything Alice does locally.
No. Communication. Is. Possible. With. Quantum. Entanglement.

Anywho, the rest of the article is great. However, let me try this little idea.
I've got an array of LEDs, positioned like so:
v v v v v v v v v v v v v v v v
and pointing at the bottom of the LEDs. Now, I send a signal from near where the left one is to the far right one, then to the one just before it, then to the one just before that, and so forth. If I do this fast enough, the signals will arrive all at the same time-but moreso, if I do it just slower than that, it will appear to be a single red light moving faster than c.
What are the applications of this astounding faster-than-light travel?
Zero, zip, zilch, nada.
See, quantum mechanics isn't really applicable to psychology. Quantum mechanical phenomena may be implicated in the functioning of action potentials, and it wouldn't surprise me if they affect neurotransmitters in entangled ways. But saying that quantum mechanics connects human brains is like saying quantum mechanics connects rocks. They're completely different objects which happen to look similar. Bose-Einstein and Fermi statistics apply only when objects are indistinguishable.

That has little bearing on the idea that reality is produced by consciousness, not the other way around. I myself have thought of that before. But quantum mechanics, by the correspondence principle, is simply not applicable at macroscopic levels.
Eurgh. I've explained things poorly. Feel free to ask for clarification wherever needed.

#19375 1 2008-03-03T04:32:53Z scythe33

Below is my prescribed title. It's not the biggest paper I'll turn in all year, but my teacher bet me that I wouldn't do good on it. Naturally, I'm determined to prove him wrong. So, please give advice on this paper as much as you can. The topic is below: "Evaluate the role of intuition in different areas of knowledge". The word limits are 1200-1600.
Ideally, a prescribed title includes extensive personal interaction and a thorough analysis of counterclaims; the antithesis of modern journalism. In particular, I'd like to see the ethics section get more polished, since it would probably surprise him (I've got a similar reputation in real life as I do here).
As always, thank you for your time and effort. If you don't bother to edit the paper, read it anyway; my prof said it was enjoyable compared to most other people's.
Prescribed Title



Evaluate the role of intuition in different areas of knowledge

Mason **** ****
12/12/07

Word Count: 1280



Intuition is one of the less easily-copied aspects of human behavior. It can be defined roughly as belief without thinking-though this provides a somewhat cynical idea of its applications. A somewhat better definition may be the direct perception of substance, what Robert M. Pirsig referred to in Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance as a sort of romantic view as opposed to the classical view dependent entirely on deconstruction. One might humourously quip that to understand intuition requires intuition. However, though difficult to define, intuition nevertheless plays a part in almost all human activity-and as a result in many fields of knowledge. Some major issues arise with the direct application of intuition-most importantly, the lack of verifiability of the source of knowledge and any personal biases of the intuiter. These gaps in the utility of intuition can be bridged in various ways, and so intuition typically plays varying roles in different areas of knowledge.
Mathematics is rarely regarded as an intuitive pursuit. Indeed, the foundations of mathematics are commonly considered some of the most firmly based in logic, and mathematics falls definitively on the classical side of what Pirsig called the dialectic split. Mathematical proof insists on complete certainty, which is not a hallmark of intuition. However, the process of proving a statement in mathematics is rarely straightforward; many statements do not give immediate clues as to their truth or falsehood. It is in this application that intuition may be seen to play the largest role in mathematical inquiry. Mathematicians often credit some ingenious proofs to intuition-I usually consider most mathematical proofs I write to be the result of intuition. These proofs, however, also highlight limitations in the application of intuition; my proofs are rarely the shortest or simplest way to prove a statement.
The main two knowledge issues that arise from the use of intuition are biases and the limitations of the source. Generally, in mathematics, biases are rare-a statement can be tested for veracity. As a result, the main knowledge issue that arises from the application of intution in mathematics is the source of the information. For example, in my mathematics class last year, the class was unable to solve a group problem-find the number of ways a circle may be divided by lines through a given number of points on the edge-until a friend of mine stopped playing calculator games and figured out how to find the solution. Also, Euler, despite extensive effort, was unable to prove that any given number may be represented as the sum of four squares, though Lagrange solved it rather quickly. In that way, the knowledge that one can gain from intuition in mathematics is limited by the intuition of the person.
Another viewpoint states that intuition has a significantly smaller application in mathematics. If proof is considered as the object rather than the mathematicians pursuing it, one can argue that proof, by its nature, must be an entirely conscious process. Therefore, intuition is not a source for knowledge but rather a direction, and given the counterintuitive nature of many ideas in mathematics it may be misleading as often as it is accurate. Here we see Pirsigs dialectic split: from the viewpoint of the mathematician, intuition plays a large role, while from the viewpoint of the person reading the proof, intuition plays a much smaller role. This is similar to the dialectic split in many other areas of knowledge.
An area in which the dialectic split can be particularly predominant is ethics, and there is also a divide between views on the role of intuition in ethics. Unlike mathematics, biases are frequent in ethics; in particular, historical and regional bias, and these are evident often in intuitive ethical concepts. For example, many people today see the practice of dueling as inherently barbaric, while in the 18th century, it was rather common. Historical and regional bias therefore presents a significant barrier to the application of intutition in ethics. Also, expectation influences many peoples ethical judgements; in America, where alcohol use is widespread, many people view the sale of alcohol as less morally questionable that the sale of illegal, though safer, drugs such as LSD or marijuana.
However, intuition can play a role in ethics. Nietzche argued that objective ethics are impossible, and that therefore all ethics must be considered from a particular perspective. Nietzche argued that It is our needs that interpret the world; our drives and their For and Against. In this view, a bias is not only inevitable, but a necessary part of ethics. From this view, the biases in intuition are as meaningless as they are inevitable. On the other side of the dialectic split, one might argue that ethics are real, and that the biases inherent in intuitive ethical judgement are not acceptable. Proponents of this view might argue for ethical objectivism; however, this raises the question of how effectively ethical questions can be resolved by reason alone. One major strength of intuitions role in ethics is the ability to answer questions which are difficult to answer from a rational perspective. This raises another question-what is the source of this judgement. If I am ever faced with the decision to take few lives to save many, such as in the famous problem of the trolley about to hit five people-yet I am able to divert it so that it will only hit one, I intuitively believe that I ought to save the five people and kill the one. However, I cannot explain how I make this decision.
Another area in which intuition has variable applicability is the natural sciences. Leo Szilard, for example, famously invented the idea of a nuclear chain reaction while waiting at a traffic light-a friend of his remarked that the hardest part of that story to believe was that Szilard actually stopped at a traffic light. Much of theoretical science occurs in thought experiments, which usually apply intuition to reach their final conclusions. However, these are occasionally found to be simply wrong, highlighting an important knowledge issue: in science, intuition is not the intended source of knowledge. This is one of the most prominent issues in the application of intuition to scientific inquiry.
Another important issue is personal bias. This can be evidenced no better than the famous thought experiment which implied quantum entanglement-action at a distance-which Einstein used to imply that quantum mechanics is an incorrect theory. However, experiments later showed that Einsteins original conclusion was correct; action at a distance does indeed occur. It is likely that Einstein may not have been so convinced had he not already been attempting to invalidate quantum mechanical theory.
These issues usually cause people to believe that intuition has no suitable role in the natural sciences; experimentation ought to be the norm. However, as Robert M. Pirsig pointed out in Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, the hypothesis step of the scientific method cannot originate from experiment. This idea supports the use of intuition in the natural sciences.
The main knowledge issues that arise from the role of intuition in various areas of knowledge are the sources of knowledge and the biases in the knowledge. These are closely connected; intuition is said to come partially from a persons mind as well as from the idea it concerns, and therefore knowledge gained by intuition will necessarily carry biases. Also, the mental mechanisms of intuition are not fully understood; it is not known where this knowledge comes from. These views are consistent with a classical, deconstructivist perspective according to Pirsig; from a romantic perspective, intuition has more validity, and biases are less important. In either view, intuition continues to have a significant role in many different areas of knowledge.

Quote: Something Awful Page titled; "Second Life Safari" by Chris Peterson
Second Life Sucks

Saturday, December 16, 2006 Update by Chris "Petey" Peterson
In The Interests Of Full Disclosure, I Am A Gigantic Dork

Internet, let's keep this between me and you:

When I was eleven, I coordinated my braces with the colors of upcoming holidays. I wore a fanny pack--in the front--with extra pencils, tissues, dental wax, and eyeglass cleaner. I ate garlicky croutons for snack every day and avoided breath mints as assiduously as others avoided me.

I had a crush on a girl named Claire in my karate class. When we practiced throws, I'd put my hands around her waist, freeze up in delight, and end up lying on my back with nary a breath of wind in my chest and my eyes doing that annoying plate-eyed swooning manga shit.

For a long time I was an active member of not one, not two, but three Linkin Park fan messageboards.

Let's not discuss my Harry Potter fanfiction addiction.

See, I'm no stranger to sucking. I'm a veritable connoisseur of crap. Much of my childhood was a series of misfortunes, interrupted by instances of ineptitude and short spells of mere failure. Nevertheless, the mindshattering awfulness of Second Life still amazes me. A lot of people complain about the technical problems of the game, but in fairness very few applications can handle a 100% membership increase in two months without hiccuping.

Sure, navigating Second Life feels like swallowing an entire can of dry tuna fish in one ill-advised gulp. Why would I choke down old albacore? Because I'm too cheap to buy a meal plan and it seemed like a good idea at the time. In any case, if that analogy were accurate, the whole harrowing experience would end one giant, bone-crushingly explosive shit later. But it doesn't.

No, the people that use Second Life bother me. Those people suck.
The Internet Explained: People Suck

Not quite everyone in Second Life sucks. For example, most of the goons who do the Second Life Safari screw around in a harmlessly madcap fashion. The people who take Second Life too seriously ruin it for everyone else. The furries that ban you from their land when you conjure one too many giant psyduck prims. The pedophiles that become upset when you don't recognize their behavior as a socially legitimate form of sexual expression. You get the idea.

The Internet does a lot of good for the world. For instance, it lets scientists design supercheap laptops for African children so they can pirate pornography and pop music like civilized folk. But it does a lot of bad, too, like inspiring weirdos to think they've a right to be free from ridicule, an assertion Linden Labs supports. I've always felt that ridicule can be beneficial. Hell, if I'd never been made fun of for being a loser in junior high, I'd still wear sweatpants everywhere. But that's beside the point.

Internet communities attract psychos like moths to the flame, only without the satisfyingly climactic moment of self-immolation. For years, they've masturbated to Sonic all by their lonesome, so adding even ten people to their crazy little cult makes it seem almost mainstream. The fact that you can script or animate just about anything in Second Life makes it about ten times worse than the rest of the Web. In the past, reality confined disgusting desires to the dreams of deviants. Now, by playing puppetmaster with avatars in Second Life, these sad souls can "live out" their fantasies. They think they are their avatars.

The Internet convinces me that the problem of the human condition is not evil but stupidity. Like minds attract, and the strength of that attraction is inversely related to intelligence. If it weren't for gelato--a delicious Italian delicacy which naturally repels stupidity--mankind would have wiped itself from the asscrack of the earth long ago. Most medical experts agree that morons naturally exert a tangible force against two things: Dostoyevsky and gelato. Don't believe me? Smear a copy of Crime and Punishment with peach gelato and visit your local community college. You'll fly higher than the local Cannabis Reform Coalition.

And that, my child, is how zeppelins came to be.
A Few Words About Virtual Rapecocks

In Second Life, your unmolested avatar enjoys an androgyny envied by David Bowie. If Second Life aimed to further social progress or incubate new business models, this sexlessness would be an asset, since it eliminates gender bias.

Imagine a world of androgynous agents, each blind to the other's actual inadequacies, purely pragmatic in their behavior. It's beautiful, in a bleeding-heart, sociology major type of way.

Unfortunately, the virtual sex industry is alive and well, as we've catalogued in previous updates. Sure, you may be a mouthbreathing needledick in real life, but in Second Life it costs mere pennies to equip yourself with a massive member Mandingo would envy.

The digital dicks industry is thriving. The sheer size of it must merit some special server-side attention. I believe that somewhere, ensconced within the vast, gelatinous bureaucracy of Linden Labs, there lives a neckbearded programmer. With hairy palms and oily skin, he furiously designs, tests, and optimizes a penile physics engine. I will call him Roger.

Roger's greatest childhood fantasy was to rub Neosporin on a dog's dick. He saw his friend Evan do it once and it was totally hot. But after PETA put him on its' hit list, Roger went underground and investigated the science behind simulated scrotums.

Of course, every man knows that even in real life a penis is only good for three things: fornication, urination, and carrying an extra bag of groceries when your hands are full. I always ask for plastic for exactly this reason.

What good is a cock that only exists in your computer? This brings me to my next point, which is that
Everything I Know About Sex I Learned From An Old Jewish Man

Growing up, my best friend was my neighbor Josh. He didn't have a choice in the matter--his family moved in next to mine, and while familiarity breeds contempt we were both too lazy to find friends elsewhere. Good for me, though, because now I had a friend, and he had a backyard with delicious cherry tomatoes ripe for the taking. They blamed it on deer. Suckers.

After his bar mitzvah, when the whole shebang was winding down, we sat on the steps of the synagogue talking about life, love, and whatever else we could think of. Engaging in serious discussion is difficult when you're distracted by aged alcoholics dancing with chairs and yodeling the background.

Anyway, this ancient relative of his came toddling out the door. When I say ancient, I don't just mean old. I mean literally antediluvian. This guy did Pilate's taxes.

"Josh," he croaked in hoarse tone harshened by epochs of usury, "Josh, I have something to tell you."

"What's up, great-uncle Bernie?" asked Josh, clapping the stooped octogenarian on his gnarled back.

Bernie smiled a hoary smile and wheezed into Josh's ear. "Never date a flat broad. There's nothing to hold on to."

I sometimes wonder what great-uncle Bernie, that primordial paragon of sexual virility, would think of Second Life. Would he appreciate the "erotica" of Players, the Second Life pornographic magazine? Would his clubbed fingers feverishly guide him towards "the best little whorehouses in Second Life"? Would he assume the identity of a younger man and peruse the wares of Strokerz Toyz, brainchild of peerless penis programmer Stroker Serpentine? Would he slowly succumb to the tender touches of Cardie Mahoney, Second Life's most esteemed cum dumpster? Or would he prefer the forbidden fruit of furry Axeonos Fluffball, admin of furnation, who demurely divulges that she "doesn't yiff while dressed like a lolita"?

I sometimes wonder these things, and then imagine Roger programming, with autoerotic precision, the aerial trajectory of an old man's money shot, arcing through the ether before settling, with a robust THWAP, on the primly poised lips of a pixellated prostitute.

And then I wonder why I am cursed with wonder at all.
Prokofy Neva, Lunatic-At-Law

The legend. The myth. I'd say the man, but I don't think anyone really knows what to call Prokofy these days. Suffice to say that Prokofy Neva is not so much a person as an experience. A way of life. Once you go Prokofy, you never go back.

Prokofy Neva is like that one superintelligent person you knew in high school who aced every test but also wore fairy wings because she thought she could fly. She believes, with equal earnestness, that the right to free expression is inviolable and that "diminishing [the seriousness of virtual rape in Second Life] is part of what minimizes rape in general," encompassing the entire political spectrum in a single mighty mindfuck.

She is the Julian Dibbell of Second Life. Sometimes, I agree with her, but mostly I just want to launch her out of a catapult into an ravine filled with large, uncomfortable rocks.

She may be the best example of how Second Life melts your mind. A former sociologist who studied the oppression of Soviet women, onetime human rights advocate to the U.N., and executive director of the International League For Human Rights, she gave up effecting change in the real world to become a transgender landlord in Second Life.

I actually have a sort of morbid respect for Prokofy. She has a keen legal wit, but flails her formidable intellect about like an epileptic at a rave. Still, if a law professor with three degrees can be suckered by the Nigerians, is it so hard to believe that something in the Russkie water made Prokofy go a bit wonky?

I think Prokofy and I agree on certain philosophical points. Where we differ--where Prokofy and most people differ, actually--is the seriousness with which she approaches what is, was, and always has been a video game. But I guess I'll never know, seeing as she banned me from posting in her blog after I laughed at her for avowing that "the avatar has reliably been found to be a window to the soul; and that communion of the souls is possible in SL in ways that aren't so religious as to be off-putting, nor so hippy-dippy as to be meaningless. It's real."

Update 12/26/2006: Prokofy has apparently sued me for libel for this post. She argues that she is "currently", not "formerly", involved with effecting change, and that "I work in causes and projects that a lame little asswipe like "Petey" can't even begin to comprehend." Good for her if it's true. It doesn't change my opinion--which, of course, you should all assume these features to be--that she's crazy.
Geeks Shan't Inherit The Earth

CNET just published an article about IBM establishing itself in Second Life.

Big Blue meets grey goo.

This is where I get back to talking about Second Life sucking.

I've spent some time in Baku, the infamous goon stronghold in Second Life. It's a wild and zany place that changes by the moment. I've sat in a hot tub next to Roger Rabbit and BASE jumped with Santa Claus. If you can code creatively, Baku is a place where you can realize your ridiculous fantasies in a community that understands it all to be a big joke.

But I wander outside Baku and into wedding parlors where debutante doppelgngers become betrothed to handsome husbands. Into a virtual Nike outlet, where people buy virtual Air Jordans. Into Reuters, where a preeminent international news agency actually pays someone to ignore crime in China, starvation in Sudan, and insurrections in Iraq in favor of reporting on studies that conclude "there is a strong correlation between well-being and success in Second Life and well-being and success in real life.

Prokofy Neva said that "geeks who sneer at people [in Second Life] who shop, or who drive SUVs, or have cybersex online, are going to be Missing the Moment."

Count me among those missing the moment, then, because digital dongs aren't my idea of a good time. While I'm out watching my Second Life pass me by, enjoy this entirely NWS video of Harry Potter discovering the carnal pleasures of simulated sex shops. See what I've been missing? Me neither.

It doesn't matter how it's done; input energy will *always* exceed output energy.
Here's one possibility:
H2O + CO + heat ---> CO2 + H2 (Water-gas shift reaction; one of the most important simple reactions)
2*CO2 + heat -----> 2*CO + O2

Quote: Shark, May 12, 2008 05:54 pm
Any chance of getting some help, guys? (*cough*cough*SCYTHE33!*cough*cough*)

Just treat the complexes as if they were metal ions. Diaminesilver is (NH3)2Ag+, but we'll call it Da+.
DaCl + HNO3 <----> DaNO3 + HCl
Diaminesilver should be easy enough to figure out, by the way.
Di + amine + silver
^ ^ ^
2 * NH3 + Ag.
Ammonia coordinates to silver (I) because ammonia is a Lewis base, while silver (I) is a Lewis acid.
Complex formation is a whole different ball game. As I recall, only two amines coordinate to zinc, but it should be on your information sheet.
Zn(OH)2 (s) + 2NH3 (aq) <------> Zn(NH3)[2+](aq) + 2(OH)- (aq).
Just find the complex ion, determine the charge on the metal, and you have this basic equation:

MeAn (s or aq) + Lg (aq) <---> Me(Lg)[n+](aq) + An[n-](aq)
where Me is the metal, An is the anion, and Lg is the ligand. You'll need multiple metal ions, anions, or ligands depending on the equation, of course.
Or, that's how I recall it.

#20397 1 2008-06-01T21:52:12Z scythe33

These represent the opinions that I could remember when I wrote this post. I have plenty of other ideas about what should be where on which list, but I couldn't remember them at the time. My memory is going at sixteen.
Also, things people already don't like (say, oil companies) and things people already like (say, Wikipedia) are not included. What's the point of me saying "I agree"? This is full of "I disagree", damnit.
Things scythe33 approves of:
1. Patagonia
If environmentalism were a competition, they'd outrun everyone and refuse to compete. Patagonia can claim partial responsibility for more revolutionary ideas than most companies have products; they were the first to break the traditional corporate culture, the first to use polyester for climbing and hiking wear, the first to use epoxy in surfboards, and the list goes on. They're also brutally honest; despite being one of the cleanest companies around, they'll admit upfront that every product you buy from them causes environmental harm, so they ask you to limit your purchases. I could say more, but I don't damn feel like it, and they can really speak for themselves.
2. Linux
Needs no introduction, does it? Continuing to outperform everyone else in just about everything, and doing it for free, allowed this one to have a high spot on the list. Serving as the inspiration for dozens more open-source projects doesn't hurt, either, and neither does compatibility with the wonderful music player Amarok.
3. XKCD
One would expect something titled with large, capitalized nonsense to suck, but this doesn't. Randall impresses every time. It absolutely defies explanation, even more so than Penny Arcade.
4. Democratic countries in Asia
Take a look at this picture right here. Note how India and Mongolia are surrounded by red and yellow. Both set what is often called "a good example". India faces the challenge of controlling a billion people, and Mongolia is surrounded by two of the worst (from a "danger to the free world" standpoint) dictatorships in the 21st century.
5. Project Wonderful
It's wonderful! Really, if I had a site, these are the ads I'd put up.
Things scythe33 disapproves of:
1. The People's Republic of China
I never really liked communism, I never really liked totalitarianism, and I never really liked dishonesty, so the PRC's totalitarianism branded as communism leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Extra raspberries for the block on Wikipedia. Add counterfeit products and child labor, and they've jumped ahead of...
2. Apple Computer
Apple earned its spot the easy way: piss me off. It's taken weeks to configure my music library to play on my cell phone, and it has presumably taken weeks for others, too. See, when Apple came out with iTunes, I thought they were finally over their "our software only works on proprietary hardware" nonsense, but music you buy from them will only play on iPods or a few Motorola (ick!) phones. To make matters worse, they sent the makers of the program QTFairUse (which allows music to be played on my phone), which was relatively little-known and hardly posed a threat, a cease-and-desist letter they can't afford to fight, even though QTFairUse does not violate the DMCA. Posing as the ideal alternative to Windows when Linux is several times better isn't cool, either, nor is their attempt to sell things on brand name and flashiness.
3. Gaia
As the second-biggest online messageboard after 2channel, Gaia is full of-you guessed it-4chan memes, and unlike the hate machine, they don't try and keep people from their site from spreading that crap all over the Internet. Which is exactly what happens, and all the noise drowns out the signal. Serving as the perfect bad example, they win the Third Worst Forum Award, after d2jsp and 4chan, but get on the list higher because of their popularity. Who would have thought the new Myspace would have been even worse?
4. Second Life
SomethingAwful can easily make my point for me: people on Second life are weird. Check the Weekend Web article on Second Life; I don't need to say any more.
5. Vladimir Putin
Everyone's favorite ruthless dictator with access to nearly half the planet's nuclear missiles. That's just what the doctor ordered.

Okay, I'm bored now. Writing this was fun, and damaging enough to my reputation ("but I like apple!", "hey, i visit Gaia!") as it is.

In fact, maybe I just wrote this to give Dave more reasons to make fun of me. You'll never know, will you?!

#441574 11 2008-06-03T19:45:38Z scythe33
Haha, that's a pretty cool trick, 654321.
If you want to be *really* devious, to hide a file...
1: Open it with Notepad.
2: Copy/paste the text into Word and save as a .doc
3: Compress it with dark, or any other suitable utility (hook is another one of my favorites). Give it an unsuspicious sounding name.
4: Most importantly, delete the original file. But you already knew that, didn't you?
To retrieve it, decompress, open it with Word, copy/paste into Notepad, and save with the proper extension. Voila!

Quote: Be_Happy_:), June 11, 2008 05:50 am
I don't see what the difference is. Is one like have less features or something?

Cell-phone Internet access started with the Blackberry and Treo, though usability was limited. The networks that the phone companies used to connect cell phones to the Internet improved to a second-generation (2G) and a third-generation (3G). 3G is the current standard for cell-phone Internet access-but the iPhone never had any of these capabilities. Rather, it could connect to land-based WiFi networks, which typically had better coverage (in addition to being free) than those put up by the cell-phone companies. The new phone has both 3G support and WiFi support, in a similar manner to many other smartphones (Other manufacturers quickly picked up on Apple and added WiFi in addition to 3G after the iPhone's release).
It's something that could have been easily added when the iPhone was released, yet wasn't.
